podcast.body: This "blockbuster hit" had just dropped from the number one spot when it featured Sting on harmony vocals. Sting also incorporated a counter melody later in the song, which he borrowed from a previous hit by The Police. "Just a few spots higher, a blockbuster hit by the British band, Dyer Straits, that had just fallen out of the number one spot, included harmony vocals from none other than Sting. On Money for Nothing, not only did Sting pitch in on the song's chorus, later in the song, he also sneaked in this counter melody."

podcast.body: This song was famously written by Mark Knopfler after he observed workmen at a New York appliance store watching MTV and making snide remarks about musicians. While Dire Straits were recording it at Air Studios in Montserrat, Sting, who was vacationing on the island, was invited to add harmony vocals. His contribution, particularly a riff on the "I want my MTV" slogan (sung to the tune of The Police's "Don't Stand So Close To Me"), earned him a co-songwriting and publishing credit, generating significant income. The song, along with the "Brothers in Arms" album, became a global number one hit. "Famously, Knopfler wrote money for nothing. After observing some workmen at a New York appliance store watching MTV and making snide remarks about how easy it must be to be a musician."

podcast.body: This song was rated very low by students who scored high on the psychopathy scale in a New York University study. The research explored musical preferences among individuals with psychopathic tendencies, finding this track unpopular with that group. "These same people rated songs like Money for Nothing by Dire Straits, and the next My Shirona really low, same thing with classical music they didn't like it."
